p: The Guess Gain tool tries to automatically work out a reasonable energy calibration for a spectrum that arrived with no energy calibration, or with a calibration that is clearly wrong. This most often happens with bare HPGe data that has many peaks but no source or calibration information — the sort of file where you would normally have to hunt, by hand, for two peaks a familiar distance apart before anything else falls into place.

The tool is opened from the Energy Calibration tab, under the More Actions column. It only ever proposes calibrations; nothing is changed until you select a candidate and press Use. The applied change is undoable (Ctrl-Z / Cmd-Z).

ol.li: Open the tool. It immediately searches the displayed foreground spectrum and fills the table with a ranked list of candidate calibrations.

Click a row to preview that calibration on the chart at the top of the window. The reference lines of the nuclides that candidate implies are drawn over the previewed spectrum, so you can see at a glance whether the peaks line up.

If you already suspect one or more nuclides are present, type each into the Candidate nuclide box and press Add. The search re-runs with those nuclides given extra weight, which usually sharpens the ranking considerably.

When a candidate looks right, press Use. The calibration is applied to the spectrum, the peaks move with it, and the Reference Photopeaks display is switched on for the matched nuclide(s) so you can continue checking the fit.

p: The table columns are: the rank, the fitted gain (keV/channel) and offset (keV) of the linear calibration, the fraction of the significant peaks that the candidate explains, the implied nuclides, and the strategy that first suggested that candidate (see below). A banner warns when even the best candidate explains the spectrum only weakly — treat those as rough starting points rather than answers.

The tool first finds candidate peaks purely in channel space (it does not trust whatever calibration, if any, the file carried). It then generates a large number of candidate linear calibrations (offset + gain) from several complementary strategies, and scores every one of them against a library of known lines:

tr.td: For every pair of strong peaks, the ratio of their channel positions is compared to the energy ratios of pairs of known lines. When the offset is near zero this ratio does not depend on the gain, so a matching pair immediately fixes the gain. This single mechanism captures the familiar “two peaks a known distance apart” approach, fluorescence x-ray Kα/Kβ groups, and taking the highest peak as a specific line.

The highest-energy peak is tried as 2614.5 keV (Tl-208) or 1460.8 keV (K-40); the largest peak as K-40, Cs-137, or U-235; and any peak that is anomalously wide (for HPGe) as the Doppler-broadened 511 keV annihilation line.
The right-hand edge of the data is placed at a series of common full-scale energies (e.g. 3 MeV, 8 MeV), and a set of common gains (e.g. 1 keV/channel) is tried directly.
As a backstop, the gain is scanned across the full plausible range in fine steps, so that even a spectrum with a single genuine line can still be caught.

p: The line library is built from common NORM, industrial, medical, and special-nuclear-material sources (K-40, the Th-232 / U-238 / U-235 chains, Cs-137, Co-60, Ba-133, Eu-152, Am-241, the Np / Pu isotopes, and others), the fluorescence x-rays of heavy absorbers (W, Pb, Bi, Th, U), the 511 keV annihilation line, and any nuclides you add as candidates.
Every hypothesis is judged by one common measure, so unrelated strategies compete on equal footing. The score rewards:

ul.li: How much of the spectrum it explains — the total significance of the peaks matched to a known line, weighted so that explaining all the strong peaks counts for much more than explaining a few.

How unlikely each match is to be an accident — a match in a region crowded with library lines proves little, so it is discounted by the local line density. This is what prevents a tiny gain from “explaining” everything by squeezing the whole library below the first few channels.

Nuclide self-consistency — if a nuclide is matched, its other strong lines should also be present. A candidate that claims Tl-208 from its 583 keV line but leaves the 2614 keV region empty is penalized.

Physically plausible peak widths — a match implying a peak far narrower than the detector could possibly produce is rejected outright (this, too, kills degenerate small-gain hypotheses); the 511 keV line is instead expected to be broad.

p: The best-scoring candidates are then refined with a proper linear least-squares fit to their matched peak/line pairs (freeing the offset once at least three lines are matched), re-scored, de-duplicated, and presented in the table.

ul.li: Only a linear (offset + gain) calibration is produced. Any residual non-linearity is left for you to correct afterward with the normal energy-calibration controls or a “fit coefficients from peaks” pass.
The tool assumes the full-scale energy of the spectrum is at least a few hundred keV and no more than roughly 13 MeV.
Low-resolution detectors (NaI, CZT) have few, broad peaks and give more ambiguous results; the reported confidence will (correctly) be lower, and adding candidate nuclides helps most here.
Providing the nuclide(s) you suspect are present is the single most effective way to improve the guess.
